Log-Tail Derivatives of the Location-Scale Families

Source: R/log_tail.R
ls_log_tail_derivs.Rd

Computes, in compiled code (ls_log_tail_cpp()), the derivatives of order o of \(\log P\) in \((\mu, \theta_2)\) for a family whose tail probability is \(P = G(z)\), \(z = (x - \mu)\,w(\theta_2)\), with \(x = q\) or \(\log q\). With \(g = \log G\), every partial derivative is the sum over the set partitions \(\pi\) of the multi-index of \(g^{(|\pi|)}(z)\prod_{B \in \pi}\partial^B z\); \(z\) is linear in \(\mu\), so a block naming \(\mu\) twice is zero.

Usage

ls_log_tail_derivs(distrib, q, theta, o, spec, lower.tail)

Arguments

distrib

One of the families of log_tail_ls.

q

A numeric vector of quantiles.

theta

A named list with the location and the second parameter.

o

The derivative order, 1 to 4.

spec

The entry of log_tail_ls for the family.

lower.tail

Is the lower tail wanted? A single logical.

Value

A named list, one component per multi-index of order o, in the order of hess_names() at order two.

The bases

The lower tail of a symmetric base is its upper tail at \(-z\). The derivatives \(g^{(k)}\), \(k \le 4\), are written out:

  • Laplace: \(g = \log\tfrac12 - z\) for \(z > 0\) and \(\log(1 - u)\), \(u = e^{z}/2\), otherwise, whose derivatives are rational in \(u\).

  • logistic: polynomials in \(p = F\) and \(s = 1 - F\), each taken from its own tail by stats::plogis().

  • Gumbel, upper tail: with \(w = e^{-z}\), \(g' = -\beta(w)\), \(\beta(w) = w/(e^{w} - 1)\), and each further order applies \(-w\,d/dw\); below \(w = 1/2\) by the Bernoulli series \(\sum_n n^k B_n w^n/n!\), above it in closed form. Lower tail: \(\log F = -e^{-z}\).

  • Gaussian: below \(z = 9\) from the hazard \(m = \phi/(1 - \Phi)\) and \(m' = m(m - z)\); from \(z = 9\) by the asymptotic expansion \(g = -z^2/2 - \log z - \tfrac12\log 2\pi + \log\sum_{n \le 40} (-1)^n (2n-1)!!\,z^{-2n}\), whose truncation error there is below \(e^{-40}\). For \(z > 0\) the term \(-z^2/2\) is differentiated exactly as \(-(x - \mu)^2 w^2/2\) and only the rest goes through the partition sum, which keeps the cancellation between the two out of the result.

Outside the support of a lognormal (\(q \le 0\)) the derivatives of \(\log S\) are zero and those of \(\log F\) are NaN.

Examples

d <- gaussian2_distrib()
# log S at 400 standard deviations, where the tail underflows
distributions7:::ls_log_tail_derivs(d, 400, list(mu = 0, sigma2 = 1), 2L,
  list(base = "gaussian", w = "invsqrt"), lower.tail = FALSE)
#> $mu_mu
#> [1] -0.9999938
#> 
#> $sigma2_sigma2
#> [1] -160000.5
#> 
#> $mu_sigma2
#> [1] -400
#>
